title: You Can Play All the Right Notes and It Still Sounds Wrong
description: Every adult beginner reaches the point where the notes are correct and the sound is not. A concert pianist explains what is actually missing, why no method book addresses it, and the four things that change it.
sub: You have the notes. You have the rhythm. And it still does not sound like music. This is the most common thing adults describe to me, and it has a specific cause.
image_alt: The strings and hammers inside a grand piano
cta_text: The free course teaches the sound alongside the notes, from Lesson 1:
body:
An adult wrote to me last month with a sentence I have now heard hundreds of times, in various forms: “I am playing every note correctly and it sounds nothing like the recording.”

They were not imagining it, and it was not a talent problem. It is the predictable result of how adults are taught to play the piano, and it is worth being exact about, because once you can name it you can work on it.

What method books actually teach

Open any of the best-selling adult piano methods and follow what each page asks of you. Page after page, the instruction is: this symbol means this key; put this finger on it; hold it this long.

That is a complete description of which keys go down and when. It is not a description of what the sound should be, and the two are not the same thing. A pianola plays every note correctly, in time, and nobody would sit through a recital of one.

So an adult works honestly through such a book, does everything asked, and arrives at a state where the notes are right, the counting is right, and the result is flat. Nothing in the book was wrong. Something was simply absent from it.

What is missing, mechanically

Here is the thing nobody tells beginners, and it explains most of the rest.

Inside the piano, the hammer is thrown at the string and then flies free. It is not connected to your finger at the moment it strikes. Once it is in flight, nothing you do can change that note — not pressing harder, not holding on, not willing it. The only thing your body controls is how fast the key went down, because that is what decides how fast the hammer travels.

Follow that through and several beliefs collapse at once:

  • You cannot press a note louder. You can only move the key faster. Squeezing produces tension, not volume.
  • Speed of the key comes from the arm, not from the finger working alone. The finger directs weight; the arm supplies it.
  • The only musical decisions available to you are how fast each key descends, and exactly when each one goes down and comes up. That is the entire instrument. Everything expressive is made of those two things.

A book that teaches which key and how long has given you one of the two. The other one — how fast, and therefore how loud and how coloured — is the part that makes it music, and it is normally left to a teacher standing beside you.

The four things that change it

1. Listen to a single note all the way out. Play one note with the weight of the arm, and do not play anything else until the sound has completely gone. Most adults have never once listened to the end of a note; they are already thinking about the next one. Everything about tone starts here, and it takes ninety seconds.

2. Make the phrase go somewhere. Music moves toward something and then settles. Take four bars and decide out loud which note is the arrival point, then play it so that everything leans toward that note and relaxes after it. This one change does more for how you sound than a month of new notes.

3. Let one hand be quieter than the other. If the melody and the accompaniment come out at the same volume, the result is mud — and it is exactly what a correct, evenly played beginner performance produces. Play the left hand deliberately softer. It will feel exaggerated. It will not sound exaggerated.

4. Stop the notes deliberately. When a note ends is a musical decision, not an accident of when your finger happens to leave the key. Adults think about starting notes and almost never about ending them, and it is half of what separates playing that sounds finished from playing that sounds approximate.

Why this is not an advanced subject

It is usually treated as one — something to worry about after the notes are secure. I think that is the wrong way round, and it is the single biggest structural fault in adult piano teaching.

The way you produce a sound becomes a habit within weeks. An adult who spends a year pressing keys and then tries to add tone is not adding something; they are undoing something. Everyone I have ever retaught went through that, and it is slow and discouraging work that was entirely avoidable.

Teaching the sound from the first note is not a refinement. It is the cheaper order to learn in.

What to do this week

Take a piece you can already play correctly — anything, however simple. Do not learn anything new. Instead:

  • Play the first note alone and listen until it has gone.
  • Decide which note in the first phrase is the arrival, and play toward it.
  • Play it once with the left hand deliberately quiet.
  • Record it, and then record the version you played last week, and listen to both.

It is the same notes. That is the point — you are not missing information, you are missing a dimension nobody handed you.

The forty-one lessons of the free course teach the sound alongside the notes rather than after them. And if you want to know what an experienced listener actually hears in your playing rather than guessing, record a few minutes and send it — the written feedback is free while the pilot runs, and it is specific.

title: How to Run Your Own Piano Lesson When You Do Not Have a Teacher
description: Six things a good piano lesson contains, turned into a routine an adult can run alone — including the one part that genuinely cannot be done without another pair of ears, and what to do about it.
sub: Most of what a teacher does in an hour, you can do for yourself once you know what the hour is supposed to contain. One part you cannot, and it is worth knowing which.
cta_text: The free course is structured the same way, lesson by lesson:
body:
Adults teaching themselves usually practise. They rarely have a lesson. Those are different activities, and running the second one for yourself — even once a week, even for twenty minutes — changes how fast the first one works.

A lesson is not more practice. It is the hour where you step back, work out what is actually wrong, fix one thing, and decide what the week is for. Here is what a good one contains, and how to run each part alone.

1. Diagnose something — specifically

Not “bar twelve is messy”. A diagnosis has three parts: what is happening, why, and where you can hear it.

Alone: record ninety seconds and listen back with a pencil. Write down the first three things you hear, in that three-part form. Writing them down is what forces the specificity — listening without a pencil produces a general feeling of dissatisfaction, which is useless.

Then pick one. Not three.

2. Fix it now, not “this week”

The point of a lesson is to feel the correct version at least once while you are paying attention, so that you have something to aim at. If you leave with only an intention, you will practise your existing habit more thoroughly.

Alone: take the one thing, slow it down until you can play it right, and play it right four times in a row. Slow enough is whatever speed makes it correct — if that is absurdly slow, that is the information, not a failure.

3. Decide the method, not just the place

“Work on bars 9 to 16” is a location. The instruction is: hands separately at this speed, then this rhythm variant, then together but only the first half, and here is how I will know it worked.

Alone: write the week's method on one line and leave it on the music desk. A week of repetition and a week of practice look identical from the outside and produce very different results.

4. Play something all the way through, uninterrupted

A week made entirely of corrected fragments produces someone who can play no piece from beginning to end. Self-teachers are especially prone to this, because nobody is there to make them commit.

Alone: once per session, play one piece start to finish with no stopping, whatever happens. Mistakes included. This is also the only way you find out whether it holds together.

5. Hear it done, not just described

Words have limits. A sound has none, and this is the part a book genuinely cannot give you.

Alone: find a recording of what you are learning — a real one, by a pianist — and listen once before you play and once after. Not to copy it, to know what the piece is supposed to be. Adults working from a book often have no idea what they are aiming at, and then wonder why it does not arrive.

6. Leave with one thing

Nine corrections produce none. End by saying one sentence out loud: this week is about keeping the left hand under the right. That is the whole assignment.

The part you cannot do alone

Five of those six work perfectly well by yourself. The first one does not, entirely, and it is worth being honest about why.

You can hear that something is wrong. You usually cannot hear what, because the fault is generally in the thing you are not attending to — and you are not attending to it precisely because you do not know it is there. A raised shoulder, a wrist that drops on every fourth beat, a fourth finger arriving late: these are invisible from inside. That is the one genuine function of a teacher that a book and a video cannot replace.

Two things narrow the gap considerably. Film your hands, not just the sound — from the side, at keyboard height, where the wrist is visible. You will see things you cannot feel. And let someone experienced listen occasionally. It does not have to be weekly; it has to be sometimes, because a fault caught in month two takes a week to fix and the same fault caught in year two takes months.

That is what the free feedback exists for. Record a few minutes of your playing and send it, and I will tell you what I actually hear — the specific thing, where it happens, and what to do about it. It is free while the pilot runs, and it is the one part of the lesson you cannot run for yourself.
